items.why: Clearly distinguishes the five spies who enter from the priest and armed men who remain outside.
Tests the clear sequence in which the five men take the items before the priest handles them.
The trees’ request makes the intended subjects and ruler relationship clear.
The passage directly links prosperity to the land lacking nothing.
A clear because-clause gives the reason, while the competing detail is merely background.
Jotham’s fear of his brother is stated directly as the reason he lives in Beer.
Successfully tests the difference between the relatives receiving the instruction and the citizens receiving the message.
Clearly distinguishes the Levite’s purpose from the place he later happens to reach.
The answer is locatable, but calling the conditional blessing a “request” makes the task artificial.
“Does something” is too vague and reduces the task to resolving a deliberately underspecified pronoun.
Clearly separates the reported news about people in the fields from Abimelek’s later observation.
The mother’s wording names her son, but the silversmith’s actual manufacture makes the distinction reasonably confusing.

The occupants’ deaths are plainly associated with the stronghold being set on fire.
It cleanly distinguishes the priests’ service until captivity from the idol’s different duration.

The fig tree’s rhetorical reply clearly presents giving up its sweet fruit as the reason.
The explicit purpose clause says Abimelek approaches the doorway to set the tower on fire.
Resolving “it” as the land gives a clear answer distinct from the people to be attacked.
Micah explicitly states that he expects favor because the Levite has become his priest.
“The residence the Danites visit” is reverse-engineered wording, and the surrounding region is not a clear separate stop.
The parallel references support Jerub-Baal, though “him” competes with the recently named Abimelek.
Zebul is clearly identified as the person who secretly sends the messengers.
The priest’s reply identifies the recipient, though the opening “him” lacks an antecedent within the excerpt.

Micah’s words clearly attribute the curse to his mother.
The passage clearly places the cursing during festival eating and drinking, after the grape work.
The passage explicitly gives distance from Sidon and lack of outside ties as the reasons no one rescues them.
